utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Sayers, or Mr. Naumovski, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vucina.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please give your name and surname to the Court?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I'm Srecko Vucina. I was born on the 25th of July, 1950, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After having completed elementary and secondary school, you entered university. You got a degree in electrical engineering, didn't you? You're an engineer now?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an electrical engineer, you worked for some time at the Sokal factory in Mostar, and then after that at a steam electric power plant at Grabovica, and then at the Institute for Electric Power, an advance planning and design unit at a steam electric power plant named Neretva?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. That's where I was when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, we usually tell everyone to wait for a few moments before they answer the questions that are put, because all of this has to be interpreted into the official languages of the court.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war broke out, you started working for the Croat Defence Council, the HVO, in Mostar in May 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this first period, you worked in the Information and Propaganda Department, the so-called IPD, and also as the press spokesman for the HVO in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In October of 1992, you were appointed head of the office of the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, by Mr. Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: At his personal request. He knew that I liked my own line of work, but he asked me to do this at least for one year. And since this was wartime, I did not do what I felt like doing, but like all others, I did what I was asked to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Furthermore, at the second general convention of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was held in November 1992, you were appointed president of the executive committee of the HDZ Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, after that convention, this second general convention when Mr. Mate Boban was elected president of Herceg-Bosna, tell me, please, at this second convention was some different kind of political platform adopted for the activity of the HDZ in relation to the political platform that was in force until this second convention? Did something essentially change there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Nothing, nothing in terms of the basic principles and provisions. What was highlighted was the importance of the Cutilliero Peace Plan and the clearly defined positions of HDZ, vis-a-vis Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a sovereign and independent, internationally-recognised state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can say that simply this political platform from this second general convention followed the fundamental principles stemming from the previous political platform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Exactly. What was highlighted was the importance of streamlining its activity in keeping with the times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us proceed. As head of the office of the president of HZ HB, you served throughout the existence of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna until August 1993, when the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was formed. And after the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was formed, you were no longer in that position; right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you remained vice-president of the executive committee of the HDZ BH until 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war, the HDZ was not very active, relatively speaking, and your work therefore focused on what you did through the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is to say, through the HVO and the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was, for the most part, except for the fact that there was very intensive work among the entire infrastructure of the HDZ before the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990, and also the intensive activities that were carried out after Washington and during the implementation of the general peace framework for Bosnia from Dayton. One may conclude that this political activity was either at a local level, where the war conditions allowed for this, that is to say, the scope was limited, and from time to time the central bodies met. That was mostly prior to certain talks at an international level or, after that, in terms of implementation of the provisions that were agreed at an international level and that pertained to all participants in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this normal political activity continued only after the signing of the Washington Accords; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the end of the war and after the Washington Accords were signed, on the 10th of July, 1994, you were elected vice-president of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the party's third convention; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the convention where Mr. Dario Kordic was elected president of the Croat Democratic Union of Herceg-Bosna; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was held in July 1994 in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remained in this post, the vice-president of the HDZ of BH, until 1996, and then from 1996 until 1998, you served as the general secretary of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. At the insistence of many that I should take over this post. I wanted to go back to my own line of work as soon as possible though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This wish of yours to return to your profession actually came true. Since 1998, you have been working in Elektroprivreda, the electric utility company of Herceg-Bosna, as the chief executive officer of the department of development. Elektroprivreda is the company that is involved in the production and distribution of electric power, and right now in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina there are three Elektroprivreda companies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And now I am director of the development department and I have to add something to this. The company is also involved in the transmission of electric power. It is true that there are three such companies and certain legislation should be passed at the level of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this subject matter is going to be re-regulated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, all three Elektroprivreda companies, that is to say, of the Republika Srpksa Herceg-Bosna and BiH, function legally according to regulations now as well, don't they?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Absolutely. These two Elektroprivredas, that is to say, of Herceg-Bosna and of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the territory of the Federation, Elektroprivreda, the Republika Srpksa, the territory of Republika Srpksa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vucina, at present, you are also serving your second term as a representative in the parliament of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be more correct, in the House of Representatives of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are going to be using only two documents during the examination of this witness, so perhaps this would be the right time to tender the first document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D277/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, until the document is prepared, a few words about previous events in Mostar. The Honorable Court had quite a few opportunities of hearing about this; however, we have to state that in April 1992, the JNA and the Bosnian Serb army launched a major attack against Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. In the southern parts of the Mostar municipality, this had been intensified earlier on and after certain provocations that took place within the municipality of Mostar itself or, to be more precise, the town of Mostar itself, I think it is important to mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vucina, let me mention the rules here. If counsel wants to emphasise something, they can. But as you will appreciate, we have heard a great deal of evidence in this case and we want to concentrate on the essentials as far as the case is concerned. Yes, Mr. Naumovski, unless there's something you want to mention about that attack, let's move on through the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point in time, in view of this immediate threat of war or, as you said, this true threat of war in the municipality or rather town of Mostar, the authorities in the town of Mostar were regulated in keeping with the regulations the town of Mostar ceased to function, and before that a Crisis Staff was established, a Crisis Staff of Mostar with representatives of parliamentary parties on it and the government in Mostar was supposed to be set up on that basis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The representatives of the Crisis Staff were Croats and Muslims, right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document that you have in front of you, could you please take a look at it. That is a document dated the 29th of April, 1992. That is a decision that was passed precisely by this joint body of Croats and Muslims in Mostar, that is to say, the Crisis Staff, and it relates to the defence of the town of Mostar. Could you please tell the Honorable Trial Chamber about it? Actually, the document is self-explanatory, we don't have to read it out, but who was entrusted with the defence of the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: The HVO and the municipal staff of Mostar and the members of the Ministry of the Interior in central Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph three is perhaps interesting too. It says that, "The Croat Defence Council shall consist of members of Muslim and Croat peoples and the members of other peoples and minorities who recognise the legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and profess allegiance to them," that is to say, allegiance to the province of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course the Muslims were left the possibility to set up their own armed units, so in a way, agreement was reached as to what could follow upon this date when the defence of the city started so all possibilities were open; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. However, it is important to mention that they are all put under the single command of the Croat Defence Council, the municipal headquarters of Mostar, and as far as new defence formations are concerned, after the 1st of May 1992, the command staff shall be constituted on a basis of parity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, this document was personally signed by the members of the Crisis Staff of both peoples, the Croats and the Muslims; is that right, and as far as you know, this document was adopted without a dissenting vote?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, and I know the persons who were members of the Crisis Staff; the persons who signed this document in their own hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like us to go through this document quickly, but I have to draw your attention to one detail. There are several interesting details but I think the last one is sufficient. In paragraph 9, in section 9, at the very end, that is, it says that everything that was agreed upon concerning the defence of the town of Mostar and the municipality of Mostar was actually temporary because it says after cessation of hostilities, that is, the liberation of the municipality of Mostar, and the creation of conditions for the normal functioning of legal authorities, all other questions will be regulated. And now let me try to abbreviate it. But taking into account the decisions passed by the legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So perhaps I should not lead you with regard to this. Do you agree with this statement that this was actually a temporary provisional organisation of life, work, and defence?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Right. As any other document during that period of time, it always included -- I think it is very important to point that out -- it always included mention of the temporary status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So at that time, when the two peoples agreed that the HVO, who would be proclaimed the force, were entrusted with the defence of Mostar, you were its only military force which resisted the aggression of the JNA and the army of Bosnian Serbs in the area of Mostar, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Indeed, and that is why this document was adopted and why this task was entrusted to the Croat Defense Council of the municipality of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. This decision which the Crisis Staff signed never questioned the legitimacy and the relevance of the -- and the legality of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it? That is the gist of this document.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we said that Muslim Serb members of HVO units in some of them, there were more of them in some of them, there were less of them, you said in your summary that some units had as many as 30 per cent of Muslims among their ranks, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, depending on the place where such units was formed and the ratios of the population in that area, that is how it was, but there is no doubt that it is quite accurate and that it held true of all those places where we were together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition to these, if I may call them mixed HVO units, there was also another battalion, the independent Muslim battalion, independent Mostar battalion, which from the very beginning included only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, and that was also pursuant to the decision that we've just talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in view of the higher level of organisation of the HVO, it was the HVO which extended all the assistance in armament, logistics, materiel, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. When it came to the needs of units, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a very hard time for all the inhabitants of Mostar because of the fierceful aggression, and until July the HVO fought fiercely along the Neretva Valley; you defended some 70 kilometres of the confrontation line with the army -- against the JNA and the army of Bosnian Serbs; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: It is after some difficulties in May, in June sometime at that time in the Neretva Valley from Capljina to Mostar to Konjic, the front line was established, over 70 kilometres long, and we were very successfully fulfilling the tasks stipulated by the decision and the mission was fulfilled except for some hill features which had been taken previously by the JNA and the forces of the army of Republika Srpksa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're also aware -- that is, you have direct knowledge of the fact that the HVO had already liberated from the Serbs part of the municipality of Konjic, taken the strategically-important village of Bradina on the highway to Sarajevo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. This was done by the HVO units in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, were there any plans to help Sarajevo through Hadzici, from the northern side?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I know and I had the opportunity of talking to participants who used that direction and were also acting in that direction, in a way. But I also know, from my conversations with those individuals, that they had received threats from Mr. Sefer Halilovic, commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if they continued their actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, Sefer Halilovic prohibited -- prevented the HVO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is important evidence. It's taking a very long time, and if we're to get through both witnesses, we must move more quickly. But don't lead. You said that Mr. Halilovic had issued threats. What were the threats?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: According to what I could learn from conversations with people who participated in it, the threat was that there would be an armed conflict if the HVO continued helping in the direction of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I should like to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, in the introductory part, we already said what office you held as of October 1992. That is, you were in the circle of people who absolutely -- who were conversant with the situation on the ground and were receiving first-hand information. Tell us, you personally, did you realise really the strategy of the Muslims from the information you were receiving and judging by the moves that they were making in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1992 to mid-1992, in spite of some tensions and conflicts, one couldn't really see -- one couldn't really glean the true relations on the ground. It was only later that I, as a member of the state commission, had the opportunity to visit. And from the situation on the ground, everything seemed to point at a possibility of aggravation of these relations, that is, from conflicts to open conflicts, in those areas which link the areas of Central Bosnia with the south, that is, with the south and the Neretva Valley. Towards the end of the year in the areas of the Rama, Uskoplje, the municipality of Konjic, the conflicts reached such a degree, that was why the state commission was set up with the consent of Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban, and it was tasked with visiting the ground and trying to improve the relations. However, it was evident then that according to what people from the ground were reporting to us, that there was really a risk of open conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And precisely because of such fears because of what was happening on the ground, what did you glean as the strategic goal? You have already mentioned Central Bosnia. Perhaps you should state that explicitly.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: From conversations based on such reports, and our insight on the ground, and other people who had different tasks, it was concluded that there could be attempts to take over control and conquer territories in Central Bosnia, because there were very important industrial facilities in that part, and especially those facilities which even in the former Yugoslavia were manufacturing equipment for the military, military equipment, and there were also roads which linked all those places. And in the Neretva Valley, in addition to a very important military facility in Konjic, there were also very important power-generating facilities and transmission facilities. And the Neretva Valley, as such, meant also a possible outlet to the seaside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. In those plans to intercept -- to cut those lines of communication between Herzegovina and Central Bosnia, you remember that the JNA used to have some plans, RAM I and RAM II, which said that some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina should simply be cut off and separated, one from another?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Those who were more familiar with this, and these are of course military, they -- that is how they identified the problem, because quite a number of officers, of commanding officers in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, came from amongst the ranks of those who used to be officers in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the information that you had at the time and your knowledge, was this plan still being put through, not by the JNA but by somebody else now?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: According to the information that we had and what happened later, it was absolutely identified as the operationalisation of plans RAM I and RAM II, but now by the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned Sarajevo and what Sefer Halilovic told the HVO or, rather, his message to the HVO. What was your conclusion about this? Why was this being prevented, why was the assistance to liberate Sarajevo being obstructed?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what the reasons were, except in that promotional part, because that is what we did, except that it was necessary for the domestic and international public to use the situation and very heavy destruction for a situation to represent the victims who remained in Sarajevo throughout these years and were victims of bestial destruction and devastation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in April 1992, do you have any knowledge of that? Were there any proposals to set up a joint HVO and BH army command in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. There were reports about that, and I learned about it from my conversations with colleagues who took a direct part in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who proposed it, and was this joint command set up?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I do not know who proposed it, except that I know that Mr. Zarko Tole was the person authorised by the Croat Defence Council, and I think that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was Dzemal Merdan who was the person. Unfortunately, as far as I know from that information and these conversations, it all ended in the very questionable abduction of Mr. Tole in the area of Bugojno, controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and his -- and many years of imprisonment or perhaps a year's imprisonment for him in prisons of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this joint command set up or not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your job, your duties in Mostar, you also knew what were the needs of HVO units in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina; for instance, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. While we could communicate and while we could see images, we could see that, but we exchanged information. However, with time, with the escalation of tensions in these lands, the same thing was happening in Sarajevo and in Tuzla. And what happened in Sarajevo is the HVO units were subjected to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Tuzla there was also cooperation in the command of Bosnia -- it was under the command of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the dignity of the units was preserved. According to persons who were members of that brigade, in a very incorrect manner, in view of the HVO casualties in the early days of the defence of Sarajevo, and I will say -- and I'm putting it mildly when I say that it was incorrect, they were put in place -- in a situation to be subjected to the command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were individuals who did not want to continue that, and they simply left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to developments in Mostar. Which was one of the early serious, grave incidents in those relations between Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: At a political level, I would venture to say it was a proclamation of Muslim intellectuals requesting the withdrawal of representatives of the Muslim people from the bodies of the provisional authority in the municipality of Mostar. I think it was in the summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what about other areas?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: In other areas, I think it was very tense, especially in early autumn when there was some of our attempts, when some of our units who set off to reinforce our units in Jajce were obstructed, however, I think somewhere around Gornji Vakuf, so they did not manage to get through and help in the defence of Jajce itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, and from what you told us already about Muslim plans in Central Bosnia, what happened in Central Bosnia in January 1993. Will you tell the Court, according to information that you had, that reached you, did part of these Muslim plans come true?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Those events coincided in time with the adoption of the Vance-Owen Plan and were intensified, and unfortunately from the municipality of Konjic to the municipality of Fojnica and other municipalities of Central Bosnia, open combat took place between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, first in the municipality of Konjic and then in those municipalities. And naturally from one -- well, I could say that it came as a surprise to the majority of people who, until that moment, operated jointly and fought together against their common enemy. But the situation was rendered more complex because over one million five hundred people were in a small area, and many refugees, and this all resulted in these tensions in addition to the events that were already mentioned, and it all brought about this very fierce combat. And this caused the conquest of those areas which, until that time, we controlled as the Croat Defence Council. In part, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina succeeded; that is, it separated these areas from Central Bosnia and especially those communication roads which linked Central Bosnia with Herzegovina, that is, the Neretva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. If I understand you well, you were cut off in two directions in the direction to the coast that is Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia and in this other direction in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, and it went on in April and May in the Neretva Valley from Konjic to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was intensified, I believe, in May?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, in May it was also intensified it Mostar itself. It went along the Neretva Valley and then onward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have more precise information about this as to which part of the road between municipalities in Central Bosnia was cut off as far as the Croats were concerned, which parts of Central Bosnia were cut off?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, of course we knew about this. I think that the communications between Busovaca and the municipality of Kiseljak were cut off, then Fojnica as a municipality, except in the higher part, high altitude parts in the town as such, communications were hampered between Travnik, Novi Travnik, and towards that other side, at any rate. There were some parts of municipalities that were involved but to be sure they were split up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. Vucina, you were in Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And so the evidence -- so we can understand it -- the evidence you're giving us is based on the reports which you received; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, a few minutes ago you mentioned that you were a member of the state commission that was formed by Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban, this was sometime in October 1992. Could you just tell us who the members of this commission were and what the basic objective of the commission was but just in two or three words?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I shall try to be brief. In addition to Mr. Boro Radic, there was myself on the Croat side along with Mr. Camil Salihovic, Zijad Demirovic, and Safet Orucevic. As far as the Muslim political leadership with Mr. Arif Pasalic as a commander of the core of the Bosnia-Herzegovina a person who enjoyed uncontested authority both within his own responsibility and beyond. Our task was after the first conflicts, I think, in Rama, to get immediate insight into the situation to try to improve the situation to help those who were needy and to take action in order to pacify things. At the same time, we were in Gornji Vakuf. There were tensions there as well. Actually at that point in time, there weren't any conflicts there. After that, we were in Novi Travnik. There could be no production in a very important factory because of these tensions. We had a meeting with local leaders, that is to say, local municipal leaders and local commanders. At my insistence, we gave tasks to both commanders, it had to do with the removal of some checkpoints and also demining. Mines were placed so that the workers could not get to the factory to work. We were quite successful because we gave a deadline of two to four hours to have the proper conditions created so that was done and we left. However, unfortunately, we found out later that things were restored to the way they were before that. We did not meet in any other area, we, as the commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have already mentioned the most important facts related to January 1993 in line with what you already said, that is to say, to divide Central Bosnia from Herzegovina and that there were several conflicts there. How did things start, to the best of your knowledge, in January 1993? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: In the broader area of the municipality of Konjic, especially those villages that were very important in terms of dominating the road and also those that are facing Fojnica, that is to say, the areas of Central Bosnia vis-a-vis Herzegovina. And then from there it moved on to the entire area of the municipality of Konjic and after that, it went on towards Jablanica and at the same time, war operations started in the territory practically of all municipalities in Central Bosnia one after the other, not at the same time. This was probably the tactics involved, that is to say, to launch an attack and then to pacify the situation, to bring in peacekeeping forces, to have talks, negotiations so the intensity was not always the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, these towns, municipalities that you mentioned are all along this main road, so to speak, between Central Bosnia and the sea, that is to say, Herzegovina and then further on towards the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me something else, please. You already talked about the strategic objectives of the Muslims so let us not repeat that again but tell us in your own words, tell the Trial Chamber in your own words what happened in May 1993 in the area of Mostar and beyond. Who attacked who? When did the attack take place? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: As a consequence of what happened in the northern area, Konjic and Jablanica, the next municipality was Mostar. Of course there were certain events, certain phenomena that preceded all of this. First of all, at a political level in terms of certain requests that escalated in May 1993 turning into an all out conflict. It is interesting that within the Muslim core, first there were mutual political tensions because very influential persons who were from the very establishment of the SDA opposed to any conflict between the Croats and the Muslims in the Neretva River Valley. Then there were some changes in these political bodies, and then new persons were brought in who were not part of the SDA leadership before. Within the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the military part, the command structure involved, for the most part, officers of the former JNA. Perhaps there were some ambitions, growing ambitions to try to bring about certain changes and conflicts always bearing in mind the objective that was clearly stated in the declarations of an institution called the Muslim Council of Intellectuals which probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the specific answer to the question you posed: Who attacked who in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, I understand you wanted to tell the Honorable Trial Chamber about the political events that preceded this military action that took place on the 9th of May or rather in May of 1993 but please, could you give a brief answer to the question that I put. Who attacked, when, and what happened in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do apologise. I don't have experience with this kind of work, but it is certainly difficult to understand these events too. The conflict broke out on the 9th of May 1993. According to the information that was accessible to us later, I don't know when others had access to it. It was clear that such orders were issued to the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina considerably earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps this is the right time for us to tender our second piece of evidence, our second document, and the last one in terms of examining this witness. While we're waiting for this document to be distributed, the one that we're going to say a few words about, Mr. Vucina, just before this attack, do you have any immediate knowledge concerning the behaviour of Muslims who worked in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Partly, yes, in relation to the colleagues we knew. Most of them wanted to get some kind of leave and go to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was before the attack?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, have a look at this document that is in front of you. That is a document -- perhaps the time is right to give the document a number too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, a number please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D278/1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Vucina, is one that you found in Mostar after these events, truth to tell, it is dated the 19th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphones are on. Is there still a problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, as I said, this document is dated the 19th of April, 1993 and it is an order?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us? Can you hear the English booth? The prosecutors seem to be able to hear us, the bench can't.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're asking you if you can hear them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Whether you can hear it or not, the technical problem requires attention. We'll adjourn now for a quarter of an hour or take the break now for a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, the position is this: that as far as possible, the system has been put right, but it may fail intermittently. There is a technician here to resolve it promptly, but it may be that there will be problems. We'll see how we get on. Meanwhile, I propose that we sit late this afternoon, if that's necessary, in order to try and finish the witness, which means beyond 4.00. But I understand that that may cause difficulties for the interpreters. If that's right, could the interpreters let the Registry know at lunchtime, and we'll make some other arrangements. Now, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the technical problems, we were discussing this document, this order, and I said that this was the order of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the 1st Mostar Brigade or, to be more precise, the 41st Motorised Brigade. The date is 19th of April of 1993. The document is self-explanatory, but perhaps if you would look at the heading, it says "Defence Order". But to save time, I'd like to draw attention to item 1 and then item 1.2. How do you understand this, not only as a document, but also what happened in May 1993 and after that in Mostar? What kind of an order is this?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: This is the cross-section of roads from the south to the city; that is, Mostar Buna, Mostar Blagaj, an important communication. That is 1.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to cut in, but I was about to ask you: From what these items refer to, is it an order for defence or is it an order for something else? This is my basic question. Let us not go into all these details; communications, logistics, and so on.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: So close -- they take the defence position and so on and so forth. It is evident that this is active defence, as it is called or, rather, offensive, and taking of battle institutions and facilities in the town itself which are along this communication, south-north communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is of the 19th of April, 1993. In view of what truly began to happen as of the 9th of May, 1993, did these things that happened -- are they in line with this order for defence?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Mostly, yes, because it mentions here Mostar Hotel, which was a vital facility which was taken, then an attack on the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, the police administration, in the immediate vicinity of the surgery department, which he mentioned here, which was also a vital facility which was to be taken in that area, and also at operations between Semovac and Bulevar, Dr. Safet Mujic Street. It is this line or front line, it became known subsequently as Bulevar. And they were mostly in that part, in the west part, these operations were during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, this document was found after the conflict broke out on the 9th of May, 1993, and, in view of what you tell us happened in May, that it is what is contained in this defence. So what do you conclude from this? When was this operation planned?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Except that I see the date here, "19th of April," that is less than a month or about a fortnight before the moment when the conflict happened in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the transcript says it correctly. Did you say explicitly who attacked whom in May 1993 in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Well, in the early hours of the morning, there were some horrific detonations in broader areas, and they came as a surprise to many people. At this moment, according to this order, evidently an attack had -- there was a strike in some parts against the units of the Croat Defence Council and in this area, so it must have been all linked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But just briefly, who attacked whom, so that the Court has a clear picture?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: The units, according to this order, the units attacked in these places and at these points in the town, the units which were in this area. Therefore the units of the Ministry of the Interior and the units of the Croat Defence Council were attacked by units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time when you were engaged in fierce fighting with the units of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a large influx of refugees arrived in Mostar. Could you tell us, roughly how many refugees did arrive in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: According to information gathered by those services who took care of the refugees, the number fluctuated. Sometimes there were 18.000, sometimes there were over 20.000. But whatever the case, there were always more than 15.000. And many people were warning that it is very near the front line and according to -- and under the international rule, we should not accommodate them anywhere near there. But we had no choice. Those were mostly people from the areas of East Herzegovina, from Gacko, Nevesinje, Bileca, and parts of the municipality of Mostar, along the eastern boundaries of the municipality of Mostar, and we simply had no other choice but to accommodate them either in the centre in various accommodation areas -- it was very difficult, conditions were very hard -- and some were with their relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to cut in. I do have to cut in from time to time because I should like us to move on as quickly as possible. What ethnic group did the majority of these refugees belong to?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Predominantly Muslim, the Muslim people, and part of the area of the Croat people who were from the village of Jesenica in the south and from this village of Vranjevici, that is, for 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, this influx of several thousand Muslim refugees to the area of the town of Mostar, did it perhaps disrupt the ethnic balance on the west side of the town?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Very significantly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you tried to care for them as much as possible, but did you happen to see where some of these Muslim refugees were put up, accommodated?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Well, at first, while the town was still shelled, it was very difficult to think about where to accommodate them nor was it possible. We tried to do that where there were some kitchen facilities. Subsequently we saw some people were trying or thought politically or differently about that; that they should be put, these people, in strategically important places, for instance, in the southern part of Mostar along the highway or the hostel which was west of Mostar, that is, in some places. And then this showed that it was not only the humanitarian part but also something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, it was planned elsewhere, is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just told the Court that a part of the SDA became a radical, that some other people came to head that party. Tell us, you must know that because they are people whom you knew. Did some Muslims, members of the Party for Democratic Action, because of the radicalisation of the views of the SDA, leave that party?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: It needs to be pointed out that a number of people, honorable local people, that is, Mostar-born and in a broader area, especially in the land of Herzegovina, were against any tensions, let alone conflicts between the Muslim and the Croat people. I can and I think it is difficult -- mentioning Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, Dr. Hadzi Huseinovic from Konjic, all of them from the very beginning were founding fathers of the party and also had some other friends in the SDA who, within this political leadership, were qualified in a manner which was not correct because they did not want a conflict. Some of them were relieved of their duties, some left it of their own will and they embarked on founding another party which was mostly concentrated in the Neretva Valley, that is, the Muslim Democratic Party. Dr. Hamica Muftic was one of its presidents, and it brought together people who worked in the agencies of the provisional executive during the conflicts, after the conflicts, and now, and my respects to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You did mention some names in your summary. Mr. Zulfo Robovic, Mr. Edin Omeragic, was there, Zlatko Udovicic, so they were the members of this newly formed Muslim Democratic Party that was active in Mostar; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Quite. And were amongst the most prominent members of the Party for Democratic Action before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, very well, thank you. Now that you mention it, you say that some of them also held some offices. You mention in your summary the office of Mr. Zulfo Robovic. What did he subsequently become in the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: After the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan and the foundation of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, he was the minister for reconstruction and development in the government of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. All those people that we have just mentioned are Muslims, just to remind the Court, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move on to paragraph 16, Your Honours. Then there was this cease-fire agreement between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban in May 1993 and after that, you knew how the situation was developing regarding the military action in the Neretva Valley. What was the conclusion according to you, of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did the fight going on in that part or not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: That meeting took place in Medjurgorje, I believe, with the moderation of international peace forces. After that, the intensity of these clashes was not as high and it was beginning to calm down, because it was obvious that there was no possibility or a chance to militarily make a break through towards the western part of the municipality and in -- and then deep into the Neretva Valley towards the coast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did this agreement result in the conclusion of peace and cease-fire in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina or not? What was the situation in Central Bosnia for instance?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: It was to be a comprehensive agreement and it was supposed to cover all areas. Unfortunately, as many others before it, they were not particularly effective and limited. In Central Bosnia, fighting was even more intensive, it even escalated, but it began to abate sometime on the eve or right before the Washington Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move on because we are under the pressure of time, so let us try to make as much progress as we can. In this case a great deal was said about Mr. Kordic having the rank of a colonel. Tell us, please, do you have any knowledge as to the circumstances, how and when was this rank conferred upon Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Not only that I have knowledge about this, I directly participated in this. Of course alongside Mr. Bozo Rajic on an occasion, we even had telephone conversation with Mr. Kordic who informed us we talked about who was doing what, and then he informed us about his participation in some talks which I think were taking place at the Butmir airport, and about the general position about all those involved in the negotiations and his personal status. Mr. Rajic and I then, on the basis of some experience in World War II, and I don't know if somebody perhaps prompted us to do that, but there was some examples when the President of the United States of America would authorise somebody who was a civilian, not as a military person, to have some status in those talks. So on the basis of this, Mr. Bozo Rajic and I personally, I think, proposed that his position in these talks vis-a-vis others in those talks should be accorded some weight, and I think that after this conversation with us, Mr. Boban with him resolved that in a conversation with him. And in this regard, I do not know whether Mr. Boban -- at least I do not know, and I cannot know with certainty they did procedures such as did exist under the regulations should be when they are published in official gazettes, because it was within the competence of the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please slow down because we are making the job of the interpreters very difficult. So if as I understand you, it was an oral decision of Mr. Boban, not a written decision?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us, did Mr. Kordic have any military training, any military training, any military knowledge, any expertise in this?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Knowing what faculty he graduated from and what is accessible to me, I think that Mr. Kordic had absolutely no skills, no training, no qualifications in that sense, nor is he a professional soldier. So that in this regard, I do not think that he nor could he be in any chain of command or any other activities in this sense except this honorary title.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us that Mr. Boban took this oral decision. You never saw in writing anything and that, in itself, means that it was never published by the official gazette or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, these negotiations of the mixed working group in Sarajevo, since the participants were persons with certain ranks, it would seem that they were simply military negotiations in the military sense. Do you know what they were negotiating about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, if you could make your questions shorter, we would get on. Also if you put less leading material in it. Why was it necessary to give him a rank, Mr. Vucina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vucina you have heard the Honourable Judge put his question.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to mention this example because as we talked to him, we concluded that in relation to a certain composition already existed there, his position in these talks would be stronger and different if we were to use, at least, that was our assumption, some experience that existed during the Second World War and if we conferred an honorary rank upon him. That is the only reason why we then assessed that that would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to belatedly object to the characterisation and the speculation about the practises during the Second World War. This is complete speculation. There's no basis for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask about that, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A brief question, Mr. Vucina. What was discussed at these meetings that Mr. Kordic attended; do you know, the talks that were attended by Mr. Kordic as honorary colonel?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Not really, except for his brief communication with us on the phone. I think it was certain directions and the opening of certain routes that was discussed. I would qualify this as general purpose matters rather than something very specialised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "specialised".

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Well, in that sense, I mean it's not that it was something exclusively military. I think that it was of general significance for the functioning of life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. For a considerable amount of time, you closely worked with Mr. Mate Boban. While you were his chief of office, you had maximum insight into his work. Mr. Kordic as one of the two vice-presidents of the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna, did he have true power? Did he have true authority to issue orders, to plan things, et cetera or was this done by someone else?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: According to the decrees, the regulations that governed everything, the only person who had real authority was the president of Herceg-Bosna. There was not even an institution that would regulate what would go on in the case of his absence. In that period, according to the regulations that he drew upon, especially in terms of responsibility and then also in terms of powers, all of this was in the hands of the president. He signed documents and generally speaking everything else that is within that framework, all of that was within his authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Irrespective of legislation, irrespective of legislation that gave powers to the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna Mr. Mate Boban, I would like to ask you, not only from a legal point of view but also from the point of view of life itself, the way things actually were, in whose hands was power, the power to decide really and truly?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: As far as I know, bearing in mind the style of the president and his decisiveness in terms of taking over responsibility and functioning and also taking into account how everything worked in that situation, especially being given communications during wartime, there is no doubt that this was taken by him only and that he was the one who made all the major decisions and had major responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in terms of your immediate knowledge and experience, did Mr. Kordic belong to this group of persons who were the very top with President Boban when decisions were made. Was he a person who Mr. Boban would consult in terms of major decisions?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: In terms of his very own system of work and as far as this military part is concerned, the only person who came there in terms of his office and in terms of his style of work was Mr. Bruno Stojic, the head of the defence department, and also the chief of general staff. I doubt that anyone else was involved in consultations let alone decision making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You attended some of these talks. You are familiar with the telephone conversations between Mr. Boban and Mr. Kordic, of course, while there was still a telephone line. What could they have talked about? What did Mr. Boban talk about to Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Of course I don't know the number; it is hard to say, but I think that this took place from time to time. As a rule, this would happen when Mr. Boban, the president, would come from some international talks or when he was preparing these international talks. They wanted to have information exchanged or, rather, to get information from Mr. Kordic about the situation on the ground, perhaps, when the situation would allow that. That is, in the sense of political judgements, immediate information, and also carrying out what was assumed as an obligation during these international talks so it is only with regard to those matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the organisation of administration, civilian government in Herceg-Bosna, who did Mr. Boban communicate with if he did communicate with anyone?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: In terms of the rules governing the functioning of temporary civilian authorities, he regularly communicated with Dr. Prlic, perhaps with Mr. Anto Valenta as well, who was in the relocated office of the civilian authority of HVO in Central Bosnia. From time to time, he would talk to certain ministers with regard to particular matters, because I know that they would come to his office and they would be there, and possibly he talked individually to some of these persons who carried out these duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question related to the work of the Presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. Did this body meet more often, less often? Did this body have a significant role in reaching fundamental decisions such as those that were passed at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: From the time when I took this over at the request of Mr. Boban, and it's very important to take that into account, that is, October 1992 onwards and until the establishment of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, that is what the circumstances were. There were war operations going on. It was very difficult to get people together. Perhaps there were some other kind of consultations in some other ways, but very seldom. I don't think that there were very many opportunities, if any, when this body would meet. I mean the impossibility of circumstances made this the way it was. Mr. Boban had to take over additional responsibility in terms of his very functioning as president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to what you said a few minutes ago, that Mr. Kordic took part in the work of this joint military group in Sarajevo, do you know, from the information that you received -- and, after all, you were at such a level that you did receive quite a bit of information -- did you ever hear of Mr. Kordic taking part in negotiations at some local, regional, or international level? Had you ever heard of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: In the period that this refers to, that is to say, the period when I held this particular post, as far as I know, at least in terms of immediate contacts with him and in terms of reports, I don't think that at any one of these levels he participated in any capacity. As for other things, I know about other persons who took part in that, but I think that he, as a person, did not accept it during this brief part when he conducted these talks at the Butmir Airport, which is what you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Honourable Trial Chamber what Mr. Kordic did, what his political task was in terms of these international plans; for example, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan or some other plan? It's all the same.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Unlike most of us who had these party duties, he had a particularly difficult role to play, for the reason that he was one of the vice-presidents of the party and he was from -- he was the most prominent person, in nominal terms, from that part. And as far as the peace agreement is concerned, he had to familiarise part of the persons involved with the obligations that stemmed from the plan in terms of our cooperation, cooperativeness, and the implementation of these plans. And I must admit that they were increasingly difficult for us and increasingly difficult to accept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his role on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Since communication was at that time relevant to that part only, there were possibilities for him, as vice-president. Perhaps he would have been in Mostar too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who explained to the citizens of Central Bosnia the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan which, as you have been saying, was not very favourable for the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. Mr. Vucina, you were asked what Mr. Kordic's political task was. Now, I don't think you really answered that question. Could you tell us what his task was? Or if you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me this opportunity to explain this fully. It would be a pity to miss out on the most important things. His task was, in very difficult circumstances, as far as the Croat people and their political leadership in Central Bosnia notably are concerned, to have them accept the peace plan which, after territories were taken, was difficult to accept for us in general and especially for Croats in Central Bosnia. Without his role in this, there would have been big tensions, and I doubt that it would have been accepted as the offered plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "territories that were taken." What territories are you referring to? Or, rather, you did not say who took these territories.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: From January 1993, from the Vance-Owen Plan to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that took them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can proceed now. You mentioned the Vance-Owen Plan. Now, in your opinion, did that plan affect the deepening of the Croat-Muslim conflict in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: This is my point of view and I'm expressing it now. In addition to the aggression that expelled over half a million Croats and Muslims from areas that were under Serb control on to less than 30 per cent of the territory that we held together, this plan, I believe, is one of the causes for the events that followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why? Tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Because, according to the information received from the ground, it was obvious that some local people and also the political leadership of the Muslim people were not in favour of accepting this plan, it seems to me mainly because the area of Central Bosnia, according to that plan, in nominal terms, were called a Croat majority province.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Mr. Vucina, tell me, you took part in the nomination or, rather, the presentation of proposals concerning persons that would have certain positions in these provinces. We are now talking about Province 10 in Central Bosnia, and its capital would have been Travnik. Who was supposed to be governor? What was the Croat proposal for governor of that province?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Vlado Santic from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know this person. I didn't understand what you said. Did you say "Vlado"?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Oh, I do apologise. Mr. Soljic. Sorry, Soljic. Vlado Santic was nominated for the Bihac canton. Mr. Soljic from Bugojno, who, in the bodies of the temporary government until that conflict, he had certain duties. He was the one who was proposed to be governor of this province from the Croat side, because according to this plan, it was the Croats who were supposed to appoint the governor of this province.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Document 1997.1 [as interpreted]. This is a document that was signed or written by Mr. Vucina. The number is not right. Z977.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. Vucina. Do you know whether Mr. Kordic had any duties in the government of this Province 10?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: In accordance with this agreement, we nominated a certain number of persons for certain positions within government. Mr. Kordic was among them. I don't know whether there was any special preference involved, but I think that he was one of the persons nominated from the five who were nominated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Just one sentence. Why was it founded, on the basis of what plan?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: The Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. I think this was sometime during the summer of 1993; July, August. It envisaged the internal establishment of Central Bosnia based on the union of three republics. In order to carry out this peace plan -- we had hoped and wished that that had happened with the previous ones as well -- the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was founded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I wanted to ask you something else. The parliament of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established as well. Who were the members of this parliament?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Well, when this was established, then, according to the solutions proposed, there were supposed to be legislative bodies as well. We always made an effort to ensure, especially in this, the legality and legitimacy of the persons who were involved there on the basis of the election results of 1990. As a rule, this was our intention. Exceptionally, we would add to these persons Mr. Kordic, for instance, and some other persons who, in temporary, provisional government bodies, carried out these duties in certain areas because perhaps the representatives from those municipalities had either been killed, or were missing, or we simply didn't know of their fate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you mentioned Mr. Kordic, and this is basically the section that we are dealing with in relation to Mr. Kordic, have you ever heard, through your contacts with him and as you followed the public media, et cetera, did you ever hear Mr. Kordic say anything derogatory or anything bad about other peoples as an entire people, including Muslims as the entire people?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Knowing him as a person, knowing his level of education, knowing his profile, knowing his sincerity, his devotion to family, his culture, if someone was to tell me that that was possible, I would say it was impossible. Even during the most violent conflict, if we ever had the opportunity to talk to him on the telephone, et cetera, I never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about Mr. Kordic -- you said a few minutes ago but I'm going to ask you expressly right now -- did you ever hear of Mr. Kordic having any direct military responsibilities, that he issued military orders at any level?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: In that period during which I worked in the office of the president, I did not have the opportunity to see or hear, then or after that, that Mr. Kordic issued a military order or that he ordered any military unit, from the smallest unit onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said to the Honourable Court a few minutes ago what the authority of the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, later the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, was. You also mentioned another civilian person, and that is the head of the Defence Department, the minister, conditionally speaking, in the HVO government while the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna functioned. Since you were close to Mr. Boban, if Mr. Boban discussed military matters, who did he discuss them with?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: As a rule, with Mr. Stojic, because he held that position. According to the regulations in force, this was part of his duties and responsibilities, to communicate with the president, and also his role was to communicate with the General Staff. Apart from that, officially or in any other way, I don't think that Mr. Boban talked to anyone, least of all about the implementation of obligations that are based on regulations and are related to the establishment of the military forces of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, you are the right person and the only person one can ask that. You were very close to Mr. Boban at that time. You knew who came to see him in his office, whom he called, who called him. That was your duty, as the head of his office. Did you ever hear, ever hear, Mr. Kordic in any situation discuss military matters with Mr. Boban or that Mr. Boban, outside these military structures, issued military orders to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Well, say I was one of the persons close to him -- of course there were others -- but knowing directly the work of Mr. President, and his readiness to assume responsibilities and duties, and his style of work, and the impossibility to communicate with Mr. Kordic except possibly by telephone at times, I doubt that it was ever possible for them to talk about this in any sense, and let alone anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move a step forward. Did you ever hear Mr. Boban discuss with any other person, that is, outside military structures, military operations or about military operations and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, no. His was a responsible style, a resolute style, and he liked to observe the procedures. He observed the legislation, and he went by that. His communication was to Mr. Stojic in the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Unfortunately, we have to move on because we're under pressure of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 25, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have heard the assertion repeated in this case that your institutions, the institutions of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HZ HB and the HR HB, in point of fact excluded other people from positions of power, that they were monoethnic. Is that true, in your view?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I am sorry to hear that there are such qualifications. I can say it clearly and unambiguously -- not only myself but documents and Official Gazettes can show and document not only our theoretical option but our operationalisation -- that in different state agencies, bodies of power, all the offices in institutions of executive branches of power, and in hospitals and universities, schools, even during the fiercest of conflicts we had in 1991/1992 with the JNA and at the same time when we had conflicts with the army -- between the BH army and the HVO, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I also have to wait for the interpretation. So, in a word, in a nutshell, to try to cut it shorter and not spend too much time on it, you were very highly ranked, you are next to Mr. Boban. Did you ever hear, officially or unofficially, any discrimination referred to?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Absolutely not. And more than that, I can confirm his lasting readiness. I was a witness to his conversation, that is he asked me to establish contact with him with Mr. Camil Salihovic, a prominent lawyer, and other individuals. And he offered them to take over duties in the executive branches of power and not the opposite to that such as there is qualification that that might be his intent, and especially not the policy and especially not the programme. In no session of a body that I attended as either the head of his office or a member of his cabinet or in any capacity, I absolutely vowed safe for whatever I participated in this. It was never said in any of these talks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Camil Salihovic and he is a Muslim and prominent lawyer. He was also offered the post of the head of the Department of Justice, something like the ministry before this office was taken by Mr. Zoran Buntic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, and subsequently at another ministry which I think has to do with administration, something like that but not only to him, to other people as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in Mostar at the time in the HVO, there were not only Muslim soldiers. Let me ask you, were there any Muslim officers in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. My commander of the municipal staff of Mostar was Mr. Jasmin Jaganjac and I was his assistant for political and information affairs. We cooperated very well. It was an honour for me to be associated to him. He commanded actions for the liberation of Mostar in 1992 and we stayed close friends until the end. This is only one of the examples in my vicinity, if I can find such examples, from Posavina to Tuzla to all other areas including what they call exclusively Croat areas, that is, Tomislavgrad, Livno, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well thank you. We are moving to paragraph 26, Your Honours. As I said, you were indeed in a position to have an insight into the work of Mr. Boban and his office and you were one of those individuals who could absolutely and directly observe the policy pursuit. Tell us, did you ever hear within the institutions of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croat Defense Council, that is the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina subsequently, naturally, the HR HB, did anyone ever mention officially or unofficially, publicly or secretly, any policy of persecution or ethnic cleansing of non-Croats from the lands of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, notably the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I have already said and I want to repeat that in the bodies in which I participated officially, nobody absolutely ever mentioned, let alone talk, about the adoption of a position which would be the official policy in the sense that we were talking about. There wasn't even a hint of that let alone operationalisation of it. Not only with regard to the Muslims not only with the Serbs, or members of any other people. And if we made some major omissions regarding the -- some events, a great example, in 1992 is no doubt during the war against the JNA, the army of Bosnian Serbs, there was not a single expulsion of a Serb or a member of any other people took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This is, as a matter of fact, a curious situation. I believe you will agree with me.
