On the one hand, there was a conflict between Muslims and Croats and you told Their Honours where and in some other areas, you told us in Bihac and elsewhere, you forged together against the army of Bosnian Serbs. That was a fact.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I was happy to be able to point out that fact before this august court that not only in Bihac the same held true of Posavina, the same held true of the area of Tuzla which, in itself, says that the problem of the overcrowding of refugees, one and the other peoples and some of us, through international negotiations, could have been the cause for our confrontation regarding the territorialisation of the lands where these conflicts took place and this relates to Central Bosnia and the Neretva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this regard, the expulsions, in inverted commas, which we are talking about, Mr. Vucina, did you ever discharge any duty, any -- have any power in Croat institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Are you aware of any plan for the expulsion of non-Croats from the territories of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna? Did you ever hear of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: As a man, a practising believer, an intellectual, absolutely never. Not only that, it was really a tremendous pleasure for me whether the vast majority of people, Croats and others, who in one way or the other were involved in institutions of executive branch in culture, education or any other institution, not any one was -- or the whole Croat people or any one of us would never do -- would never show any propensity for saying things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well, we are now going to paragraph 27. We have already talked about that. You told us that Mr. Kordic phoned Mr. Boban about the international negotiations and then Mr. Kordic discharged his political duty and explained the international plans in his area, that is, in the area in which he could be active in view of the wartime conditions. I suppose there was also mention about the Vance-Owen or Owen-Stoltenberg Plan or the Washington Accords.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. It is difficult now to explain in so many words the situation because there were different conditions for Croats in different parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina following different international agreements and even if many think that the Vance-Owen Plan was an acceptable one, nevertheless, needs to remind that many Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were left outside of those areas. Although we all believe that the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna as defined by the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan was such as one of three republics with the ethnic prefix, but the majority was also against it because some areas were excluded and it was particularly difficult when, in peace talks, one would see that some areas which had been lost through war had become an integral part of the offered peace solutions. From Vance-Owen to Owen-Stoltenberg, Owen-Stoltenberg to Washington, and then especially Vienna Agreement, and then if you compare the maps, then you will see that of the 28 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Vance-Owen Plans, we've come down to a 25 in Owen-Stoltenberg's Plan, to some then 11 per cent in Washington, to only 8 per cent after the Vienna Accords, and that was only that much of the area that was defined as a Croat majority area, so it was very difficult to implement what was our task to implement. And in -- we approached all the negotiations in good faith and President Boban signed it all and we were ready to put it all through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a mistake. You said 17 point something of the Owen-Stoltenberg, but it was 18 per cent.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let us try to bring your testimony to a close -- your testimony in chief to a close. The implementation of the Washington Agreement, that is the period of time when Mr. Kordic had already become the president of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What was his role in this? Did he take part in talks with the SDA and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: As the protagonist of the political power in the Croat Democratic Union now, this is a completely different, more important role. As the president of the Croat Democratic Union, he bore additional responsibility because we were a serious political subject. To implement what had been signed at the international level, he spared no efforts to conduct the negotiations to create the atmosphere to do whatever was in his power to have the Washington Agreement implemented. And I am witness, because I was one of his associates as one of the vice-presidents and I therefore participated as a rule in all the talks between the HDZ and SDA which Mr. Kordic conducted. In terms of the implementation of the Washington Agreement, from Mostar to Vranica to Sarajevo which was still being shelled by the Serbs, and other areas, he did it with dedication because it was necessary to agree under the constitutional provisions and the provisions. In the international negotiations and agreements, one had to determine that the shares, the proportion, the ratios and so forth, and he spared no effort in doing this. There were some objectives why, on the other side, it was not the president of the SDA to conduct the negotiations to be his counterpart. We almost put an ultimatum that the other -- that Mr. Kordic as the president would appoint one of us, the vice-presidents, to conduct these negotiations, but he refused to do that and he conducted all these negotiations personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you very much. In paragraph 28, which is the last paragraph in your summary, you speak about Vienna negotiations, that is, that before the Vienna agreements, a large group of some 80 Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina went to Zagreb and met President Tudjman. You were present there. My question is: Was Mr. Kordic present there too?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: As far as I know he was not and I think he is a person who would be noticed especially as I know that from the area of Central Bosnia on behalf of the Croats first and foremost, it was Mr. Lozancic who did that. Had Mr. Kordic been there, no doubt he would be speaking on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Vucina. This is the end of our examination. Thank you, your honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Vucina, my name is Kenneth Scott. I'm one of the attorneys representing the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Scott. I would like to say hello to you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, according to what you've told us today, you were the head of Mr. Boban's office of the president for the entire existence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, is that correct, until sometime in approximately 1993?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Well, from the moment I was appointed until, as you say, I was transferred to the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is to say, not from the very moment when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was founded which was the 18th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are right, sir. Let me correct myself. From the time that you were appointed you continued in that position until the end of the community, that is, until it was transformed to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in approximately August of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this position, I think in one paragraph of your statement, sir, you characterise your role or position of essentially for all practical purposes, Mr. Boban's Chief of Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I think that it is very difficult to compare English and Croatian. We say the head of office. It is very hard for me to translate this into the mental pattern of the English language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Well, you have the English version in front of you, and I'm not going to belabour this, but in the English translation, paragraph 26 of your summary, you say you were in effect, Mr. Boban's "Chief of Staff". Perhaps it can be placed on the ELMO and would be the easiest way of referring to it. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I assume that it relates to the same thing. The operative part of the office that did what was needed for him, I imagine, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct then, sir, for the Court to understand that with Mr. Boban being deceased, that you were the highest official in his office and the highest living representative of Mr. Boban. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: After he died; is that what you said? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time, sir, perhaps I should -- I didn't say it clearly enough for you. You were the person, during this time, during which at least in the English translation of your statement, it's -- you are characterised as the Chief of Staff. You were the number one person closest to Mr. Boban on a day-to-day basis; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, within my own rights and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you very directly. Was there anyone else in Mr. Boban's office who had a higher position in his office or more direct or regular access to Mr. Boban than you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the questions that were being discussed. If it was the executive branch, then it was the representative of the executive branch. If it was defence, then it was the head of the defence department, and if it was the interior, then it was head of the office of the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I am talking about the office of the president. Was there anyone else in the immediate office of the president who was -- who had a higher position or was closer to Mr. Boban than you. It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: The answer is simple also. Not in those areas where I did not have rights and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Before you took this position, you worked in the information and propaganda department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Of the municipal staff of Mostar, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- what was your functions there? What did you actually do on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: It is a wide scope. There is a wide range of responsibilities that I had, because the war made it necessary to do different things, communication with various persons, but this was important. I was assistant commander for information within the municipal staff of Mostar, that is of Mr. Jasmin Jaganjac and at the same time it was the press spokesman for the HVO in Mostar. That is to say, that there were regular day-to-day communications with the members of the press externally while, internally, vis-a-vis certain colleagues that carried out these activities in various units, there was information about their cultural and other needs. In due time, it turned out to be necessary to create various divisions that would take care of the disabled, of the families of the killed. So these activities were expanded considerably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you because we do have to move on. When you say you were the spokesman for the HVO in Mostar, do you mean you were the spokesman in Mostar for the entire HVO organisation or are you suggesting, just so it's clear, you were only the local spokesperson?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: The entire HVO that relates to Mostar, that is the Mostar HVO. Not the HVO that was in other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we were to assume for these purposes simply to make the point that the HVO headquarters in Mostar was something like a national government of what was called Herceg-Bosna, were you the spokesman on the -- of the national government?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, because this was set up later. I imagine I understand you. I think it was the duty that was later held by Mr. Bozo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a few months after having this position in the Information and Propaganda Department, then you moved to become the head of Mr. Boban's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, can you tell the Court, you were trained and had been previously employed as an electrical engineer. What qualifications caused you to become Mr. Boban's Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: If he were alive, it would have been a question for him. I don't know. I spoke as the press spokesman, and on the basis of my other activities, he probably decided to ask me to take over this post for a short period of time. I am not qualified to make public pronouncements on my own qualifications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were close to Mr. Boban politically, weren't you, very close, and that's why he chose you as his Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever, at any time, in your experience with Mr. Boban, disagree with Mr. Boban on any matter of the goals of Herceg-Bosna or on the strategy or policy or practices of Herceg-Bosna or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Allow me, sir, to say that, politically, this was after the convention, whereas this appointment was before the convention, so my political appointment was after the convention. As for the provisions of the Croatian Democratic Union, the basic principles, I didn't disagree with anything on that matter. But as far as certain day-to-day matters are concerned, he was happy to discuss them and he was even happy to engage in dialogue that involved opposition and that is the kind of dialogue we would have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me repeat my question. Did you ever disagree with Mr. Boban on any matter of the goals or strategy or policy of the government of Herceg-Bosna as related, for instance, to the prosecution of the war?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: First of all, one cannot say that he produced war, so I cannot face that. If there was a strategy of persecution that was pronounced, I certainly would have opposed that, but that was not his policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the way, sir, where were you during this time? Were your offices throughout the time we've talked about today in Mostar or were you at any time in Grude?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: The office of the president was in Mostar. That is where I resided. Daily, weekly, or whenever necessary, I would go with him, if he was not in Mostar, to wherever his relocated office was. As a rule absolutely, the seat of his office was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that, sir, where you in fact spent most of your time from 1992 through 1994, in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Because the office was there? I don't understand your question. I am sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has nothing to do, sir, with the location of the office. Did you spend most of your time in Mostar during 1992 through 1994?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then sometime after this, you became the president of the executive committee of the HDZ-BiH from approximately the 14th of November, 1992, until 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did that position place you in terms of the party hierarchy? That was an extremely high and senior position in the party, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: According to the statute, yes, I was president of the executive operative body of the party of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you come to that position? Were you elected in some fashion or were you named to that post by Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: According to the statute of the party, the convention of the party elects its central body, and then that body elects the president of the executive body, and that is how I was elected. As president of the executive body, I proposed members of the executive body to the membership, and that is what I did in accordance with the statute of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then did you hold that post at the same time that you were also one of the vice-presidents of the HDZ-BiH party?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No. In the period from 1992 onwards, I was president of the executive council and, after that, vice-president of the executive council, so that was probably it. And from 1994 to 1996, I was vice-president of the Croat Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've said in your direct testimony that you are currently serving your second term in the parliament, if you will, of the Federation government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which political party, if you will, do you represent in that government?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: At the elections that were held now, I was on the list of the Croat Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HDZ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you had any military training or experience?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, except for the fact that I did my compulsory military service when the time came after I graduated from university. Otherwise, I have no such inclinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very briefly, sir, just tell us, what year was that that you served -- fulfilled your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: 1976, when I graduated from university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the role that you've told us about so far this morning, was it your position -- did you have any military roles? Did the work you did for Mr. Boban, as his Chief of Staff, have any military dimension?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I only did that part when I was assistant commander for Information and Propaganda in the municipality office staff in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn until half past 2.00. Mr. Vucina, don't speak to anybody about your evidence during the break, and don't let anybody speak to you about it until it's over, and that does include members of the Defence team. Would you be back, please, at half past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.28 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I'm told that, in fact, the interpreters or someone will be required elsewhere at 4.00 so we can't sit beyond 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do my best. I have to say that the Court -- I'm sure the Court must understand given the testimony this morning by this witness, he is a virtually unique witness in terms of his position with Mr. Boban, and you can expect that there is substantial material. But having said that, I will certainly go as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how many -- well, just to bring us back to where we were. I had asked you if your positions, you told us about before the recess, if any of those involved a military dimension and you had indicated your answer I believe was no, they did not. Let me ask you, sir, how many military orders did you see while you were the head of the office of the president?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Not a single military order because it was not within my field of work, so I did not see any coming from the Main Staff since the coordination was ensured by the head of the Department of Defence to the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, sir, how many military strategy meetings did you attend?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Not one military strategic meeting because that was not within my field of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings about tactical planning, military operations?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph five of your statement, sir, you say -- forgive me, I may have the wrong reference. Let me ask you a question, and in the translation, I will try to find the reference. You indicate in your statement, I believe, sir, that there was a particular order that something was either an order or characterisation that something was couched as a defensive action in a deceptive way but in reality, it was, in your view, it was something offensive. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: You mean this morning, it concerned the order of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you can give me a moment. I apologise. My notes have the wrong paragraph. All right. Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 13, sir, the last line starting on the bottom of that page, "We found the Muslim order dated April 19th, 1993 which is couched as a defensive order but indicates planning for offensive actions against Mostar." Did you see that order, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: The one that was shown today, yes, but much later, a long time after the events, and it is accessible to many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately when do you remember seeing this order?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Much later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: A year and more after -- a year and more later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I do not know who it was, but it was accessible in very many documentation offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what basis do you conclude that it was couched as a defensive order but indicates planning for offensive action?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: This morning, under item 1 or 1.2, it says explicitly that after the taking of positions, offensive actions had to be taken towards some positions and from that, it was easy to conclude what I said "active defence", as it is said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us today that your last military service was in 1976. Your jobs have no military dimension. You said you did not see a single military order during this time, not a single order, and yet you've come to court and indicate to us that you have the ability to make a judgement that a military order that was couched as a defensive, in your view, really was offensive. Now, sir, how can you say that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: On the basis of things that happened on that day and those days in Mostar. It is quite evident, it is quite contrary to what is said here on the basis of events in which I participated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, someone told you or characterised this order to you, didn't they? You reached this conclusion based on what someone has told you or suggested to you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: As we talked about the organisation of Mostar after Dayton, then one of the problems was the organisation of the central area. I participated in those talks. It was highly indicative that some of the proposals of the other sides were along these positions which are indicated in these orders so I cannot see any precedent here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, sir, because of time. You did not answer my question. I put it to you, sir, this entire conclusion -- this entire statement in paragraph 13 of your statement is just simply something that someone else has told you or suggested to you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: That was my judgement too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me, sir, how does one couch an offensive order as a defensive order? Just tell us how you would do that. If one of us wanted to do that, tell us how we would.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I cannot tell you, because I did not write that order. Presumably, if the one who asked that were alive, he would perhaps be qualified to interpret it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you some questions about your preparing to come here today. When were you first contacted by anyone representing Mr. Kordic or the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I think it was right before Christmas holidays last year, and the second time was during Easter this year. And when I was asked to come here, I saw a statement which was the product of this cooperation, and I had some minor corrections regarding the text, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This statement was different than the one that you've signed and tendered to court, the 11-page statement that you've signed? This is some other statement?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No. No, not at all, not in things that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was there a different statement? I'm not asking whether the differences matter or not. Was there some prior statement by you, before this statement was prepared, which has not been provided to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who contacted you, sir? Don't tell me what they said necessarily, but just tell me who contacted you about coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: The lawyers representing here the Defence of the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that, specifically?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Mr. Mitko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet -- in the course of preparing to come here to testify, sir, have you ever met with any person who you understood to be a representative, or official, or some agents of the government of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, not once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you ever met with any such person or representative, official, or agent associated with the Bosnian Croat part of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony before the Court is that no representatives of the Bosnian Croat Intelligence Service have ever shown you documents or provided -- done anything to prepare you for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I guarantee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you reviewed any documents in preparing your statement or making statements to the Defence at any time?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, both your summary and the testimony you've given today in some respects is quite detailed. Are you suggesting to us this was all based on memory and that at no time, since first being contacted by the Defence before Christmas last year, you've never reviewed a single document to prepare to testify?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. Based on my recollection and my judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask the usher to please hand you Exhibit D278/1 from this morning. Perhaps in the interests of time, Mr. Usher, you could put it on the ELMO and we could all look at it at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown this document this morning. Is today the first day -- first time you've ever seen that document?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: This is a translation of the order that this morning we had an opportunity of seeing in the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I apologise if you don't have the original-language version in front of you. It should be available to you there. If it is, if you want to check, you certainly may do so. Let me repeat my question. Is this the first day -- the first time you ever saw that document?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No. As I have said, I saw it much earlier, but a year and a half later, roughly, after it was written. This is a document that you can come across in Mostar with many people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other exhibit that you were shown this morning -- you were only shown two -- had you ever seen that document before today? And the usher can show you, if he would, please.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: This is an official document which was carried by the Official Gazette of the municipality of Mostar, and it was also carried by the press in 1992. So it is accessible to the public and, therefore, to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, I understand all that. Had you actually seen the document before today?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, 1992 is when I saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. At any time since 1993, sir, are you aware or have you been aware of an HVO archive or archives where documents like this and other documents are kept?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: If you mean this document, the one before me now, it is accessible to the public. The archive of the civilian authority of the provisional executive power of the HVO existed in the place of their residence, that is, in Mostar. The archive of the military structures, that is something I know nothing about. I do not know where it was kept or where it is. As for archives in general for Bosnia-Herzegovina, we tried to organise it and define the documents that should be there. Unfortunately, we failed to create an archive as exists in many orderly administrations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the archive you just mentioned of the civilian authority and the provisional executive power of the HVO existed in the place of their residence, that is, in Mostar, you said. When was the first -- excuse me, when was the last time you had access to that archive?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I did not have any access to that archive at all; it was the archive of the provisional executive authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where that archive is located today, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I am not now a part of any structure as apart from being a member of parliament, so I have no knowledge about that at all. I am only an engineer now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you are a member of the federation of parliament representing the HDZ party or affiliated with that party. Have you ever been made aware of the fact that this institution, that is the Tribunal, has been seeking such an archive or documents from an archive for a number of years? Has that ever come up in discussions with you or in the course of your official duties or unofficial?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, from the press insofar as it was accessible to everybody. Apart from that, there was no reason because I belong to no structures after I finished my work in the bodies of the political authority. I had no other responsibilities except that we could hear in the media that certain documentation was being sought related to all these cases of relevance to this Honorable Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you really can't help us, sir, by giving us any idea where that archive may be located today?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I declare, under oath, that I cannot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how many times did you have any direct face-to-face dealings with Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: In 1992, I think it was a visit of theirs while there was still some communication, we had a meeting in Mostar. It was not an official meeting. After a considerable period of time, we met finally and after that we went to Mr. Rajic and ended up at a private dinner. In 1993, I think the first time I saw him was when he and many others following the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan could, and I think we met in Grude at that time when a decision was taken to found the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Meanwhile while the telephones were in order, we would hear from each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to cut you off. I'll get to the telephone in due course, but you've told us that you may have had two or three -- in the course of 1992 or 1993, you might have had two or three direct dealings in person with Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I think. I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the Grude meetings where the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was declared, did you actually interact with him there or did you know that he was just one of a large number of people who happened to be there at the same time?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: There was a conversation at the table -- there were two or three of us -- and after that, there was a general meeting, that is, when we first saw and talked and after that there was a general meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now going to your next point, and approximately can you tell us how many times you talked to Mr. Kordic on the telephone or any other sort of wire communication; radio, telephone, what have you? How many times did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: It is difficult to say. I'm doing my best to remember, but it depended on the opportunity when we could communicate by telephone. It would sometimes be once a week, sometimes once a month. When the radio links operated, that is when the so-called packet system worked, then the reports were communicated regularly in so far as the time permitted. So this is roughly for the period between 1993 and the time when we met personally in Grude when the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was founded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, nobody is going to blame you for not having an exact number in mind, but can you give us an approximation of how many times you spoke to Mr. Kordic in this manner; a dozen times, two dozen times, 50 times?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Well, somewhere in between, around 20, I think, thereabouts as for the telephone part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was for all of 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, not 1992. In 1992, late 1992 and part of 1993 until August, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What were the nature of the reports that you received, you say you received reports, what kind of reports were these?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Well, mostly about the situation in different areas, needs of the population, events which took place, combat operations, effects and of other nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you seeing military reports?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, not in the military sense, because they have their own procedure, but as a result of military operations and what had happened, it was not a military person who wrote those reports. That was not my line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's not get -- well, whether they were military reports or not, were they reports that conveyed military information?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Not military information, but the results, the upshot of military happenings, military information wasn't coming to us, that is, to me personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these reports that you were receiving from Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: About the situation in relation to the areas, among other people, yes, from him. About his need to intercede with some other institutions, yes, we would forward that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these included, you've said a few minutes ago, from time to time, the outcome or the aftermath of military operations; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, things that had happened. For instance, loss of an area, the effects of that, accommodation of people, and everything else that would result from those military happenings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you received such reports from Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Alongside his signature, there were other people. Alongside his reports, there were also other people, because Mr. Kordic was related to one area. And we also received reports from other areas, mostly Central Bosnia from Herzegovina and wherever there were combat operations, their results, the situation, and relations that existed under those conditions. So not only from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Kordic was Mr. Boban's principal contact in Central Bosnia, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: One of the principal ones in the political sense and for some judgements, yes, one could accept that, but not the only one in the sense of overall observations, but not in the sense of the military, because in the military, he was not that at all because there was a specific chain of command which was in conformity with the Croat Defense Council depending on its organisation and it was in effect for everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- well tell us, sir, what political official or leader in Central Bosnia did Mr. Boban hear from more than Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Mr. Boban had his method and his working practice in his daily contact with people who had the opportunity to come or to travel. He would meet with them and discuss many aspects and many subjects. His style of work included this practice. He went there; we opposed it. It was his practice to receive almost everybody. This is a very broad range of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you again. My question is -- I'll just simply read it back to you. What political official or leader in Central Bosnia did Mr. Boban hear from more than Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: If you mean in quantifying terms, it is difficult to compare, but with regard to his possibilities or his accessibility, every president of the provisional executive authority in municipal council or every president of a municipal HDZ who had the opportunity to come could see him. There were people who were involved in humanitarian affairs; they also met with him. There were people who were engaged in some church affairs or duties; they also were in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that your answer to the Court is that you could not tell the Court any political leader or official who had more contact in Central Bosnia -- from Central Bosnia, excuse me, with Mr. Boban than Mr. Kordic. You can't tell the Court that.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, I cannot affirm that it was only Mr. Kordic. I can claim the contrary, that many people talked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Let's move on. How many times did you hear Mr. Kordic speak, in terms of public speaking, either live, on television, on the radio; how many times did you actually hear him speak?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: While I was the spokesman, and that was the beginning of 1992, I think that at that time Mr. Kordic had a regular practice, because that was the custom, to have such press conferences in Central Bosnia. The fragments of it would be transmitted by television screens or radio, and that was the only occasion that I had of hearing him addressing the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times; once, twice?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I suppose -- I should say more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, ten? Please help us, sir. The Court will accept -- it doesn't have to be a precise answer, but give us some idea of how many times.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, no, no, I -- those press conferences were at times -- at regular intervals when the circumstances would allow it, but not less than once a month; sometimes more often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you haven't answered my question. My question to you is not how often the press conferences were. My question is: How many times did you see or hear Mr. Kordic speak in public, either live, or on the radio, or television, or what have you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. On how many occasions on television, I really cannot give you the number. But if it was on television, I had the opportunity of seeing it and hearing it, what the television transmitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're not going to answer my question that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I don't think we can follow this much further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, between June of 1992 to approximately March of 1994, can you tell the Court, how many times were you in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Until 1994, after the hostilities ended, that was the first time I went to Central Bosnia. We were in Vitez to establish electoral assemblies, the municipal organisation of the HDZ, and that was the first opportunity -- that was the first time that I went to Central Bosnia personally, physically, when the hostilities ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately when in 1994?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I think this was in the period of the summer or, rather, it was the end of the spring or beginning of summer. I know that I wore a loud suit, for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not in Central Bosnia, sir, at any time in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: 1992, yes. I said this morning, at the end of 1992 I was on a commission, a state commission that was appointed by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban, and we were in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, in Travnik. Okay. And was that the only time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I think that that was the only time, except for the time when I went north to Usora. This was a visit that I paid with friends, to some of our people who were up there, but it was no official visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I take it, then, you've never been to a headquarters facility at a location known as Tisovac. You were never at Tisovac, were you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, not a single one of those places, especially not where there were combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever at offices that may have been used by Mr. Kordic from time to time in the PTT building in Busovaca? Were you ever at his offices there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Not at the PTT, but I slept in another building which was a motel or whatever when I was in Travnik. I spent the night there. He was busy, he had other matters to attend to, and he did not spend the night there at all in that particular motel. Only the janitor was there. I don't know exactly what the name of this place is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is in Busovaca, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: When we had that mission as a state delegation, after that, in Travnik, I spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the same trip that you were in Travnik, you were also in Busovaca, in 1992; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I spent that night there. I came there around 1.00, and we went further on in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 11, sir, you mention Prozor. Let me submit to you, sir, that there was an unprovoked HVO attack on Muslims in the Prozor area on the 22nd and 23rd of October of 1992, and you were personally present in that area a couple of days after the attack, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it was April. This is the spring of 1992, and I think that it was in October. That is when we, the commission, were there in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I said "April", it's my mistake. I don't think I did, if you look at the transcript. But in any event, were you in the area of Prozor in October of 1992 within a few days of an HVO attack in that area?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: As the delegation of the state commission, we were there, the representatives of the Muslim and of the Croats, with the assignment that we were given by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban. We were there on an official meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, there was an HV -- Croatian army general named Praljak who was also in Prozor at the same time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak was not at that meeting. Mr. -- Colonel Siljeg was there on the HVO side, and on the BH army side, Mr. Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did it ever come to your attention that Colonel or General -- excuse me, that General Praljak himself was stunned by the devastation that had been carried out against the Muslims and Muslim property in Prozor at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Although I personally know General Praljak, because he's a colleague of mine, he also has a degree in electrical engineering. I did not have the opportunity of talking to him then. Knowing his intellect and his culture, I do not preclude the possibility of him having reacted the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, there were Croatian army forces involved -- that is, of the Republic of Croatia that were involved in the attack on Prozor, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Absolutely, I have no idea about anything like that. I really doubt it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of an HV brigade called the Tigers?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: That is a celebrated brigade of the Croat army. They fought in the Dubrovnik area and liberated Dubrovnik in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any basis to tell this Court that the Tigers were not involved in the attack on Prozor in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: According to what I can know, I think that I can be quite confident of that. And judging by how the Tigers fight, it is quite sure that it was that brigade that managed to liberate Dubrovnik with such great sacrifice, and I really doubt it -- I really doubt that they would have been involved in that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'm going to move on. But the answer is you don't know; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: You can interpret it that way. But judging by what the commission ascertained, I never heard Mr. Arif Pasalic ask, and he is a competent person, at least. He never asked Mr. Siljeg or anybody else, any other participant; nor did he accuse anyone of having those units that you are mentioning present there. That is relevant for me, because that is how General Pasalic spoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your close association with Mr. Boban, did you ever hear the view expressed that it was extremely important to President Franjo Tudjman of the Republic of Croatia that the defence industries in Central Bosnia be maintained under Croat control?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, not a single time, and I don't think it was that important for some kind of Croatian military industry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recall any conversations between Mr. Boban and Mr. Tudjman where Mr. Tudjman talked about the explosives factory in Vitez and wanting to keep that under Croat control?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No. I doubt that they would have dealt in matters like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified about Mostar, sir. Isn't it true that the HVO first disarmed the Muslims in East Mostar and then attacked them in April and May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: If such a statement was true, there could not have been a war there. Had anybody been disarmed, there would have been no one to wage war against or with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, sir, is: Isn't it true that it was the HVO who attacked Mostar then? Let's put the disarming, if you like, to the side. Wasn't it the HVO which initiated the offensive against Mostar in April and May 1993?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: The units of the HVO held the front line which borders on the boundary of the Mostar municipality on the east against the Serbs throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go on and come back to that, perhaps. In paragraph 13 you say in Mostar in particular, the May 1993 conflict was set against a back drop of political conflict inspired by Safet Orucevic and, forgive my pronunciation, and Zijad Demirovic. If you want to look at your statement you can, but that's the statement that you make. That the May 1993 conflict was started as a result of political conflict. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It says so in the statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the statement you also made the point of saying that Mr. Demirovic had been, at one point, a prisoner in the same prison with Izetbegovic in the old Yugoslavia, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, not Mr. Demirovic, Mr. Safet Orucevic, and that was a lot earlier. It was before 1990, before the war, because of certain criminal offences, as far as I know, so he was not a political prisoner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's -- what was the point in including that in your statement if you can just help us. Why did you even comment at all that he was in prison with Mr. Izetbegovic at some point?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Their close encounters probably date back to that time and he has held high positions in the SDA. From the beginning and before the aggression was carried out in 1991, he closely cooperated with the Croats on this common defence, later on this role changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you talking about the conflict that you say was started as -- against a backdrop of political conflict, this the fighting between the HVO and the Muslims in Mostar around May of 1993 just to make sure we're talk being the same point in time? Yes?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, this conflict occurred within the SDA, within a core of their own, amongst themselves, and this had other reflections also. The only legitimate president of the SDA there was replaced then and Mr. Demirovic took a certain position at regional level, at the regional committee of the SDA, and Mr. Safet Orucevic, I think, was in the municipal organisation of the SDA, and then after that, there were certain political tensions and political conflicts with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What conflict inspired the fighting? I want you to explain to the Court that the political conflict inspired the fighting in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: It contributed to the overall situation that speeded up these developments. However, this occurred in an area that was to the north, Konjic and Jablanica, and this is a broader context than that that I referred to today that had to do, perhaps, with their aspirations to reach the Adriatic Sea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, it's your statement that these two Muslim men, these were political figures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your position is that these two political men caused the conflict in Mostar. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: To be more precise, they speeded it up. Not only them, not them exclusively, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would agree with us, sir, that, in fact, politicians do cause and sometimes direct fighting. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Perhaps I would rather agree with the fact that they can contribute a great deal to creating a climate in order to avoid fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you the opposite of that. Can they also -- would you also agree with the fact that they can contribute a great deal to creating a climate that promotes and causes fighting?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree, and there were possibly quite a few events and examples at local levels where some people managed, through their own efforts, to prevent conflicts from breaking out. Also, with the opposite kind of activity, they could have provoked conflicts which then actually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these politicians could cause fighting whether or not they had a military title or not, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that they are indeed that powerful. In some situations, I deem it more expedient to think that some high officers had greater ambitions than those that the situation actually allowed for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, what you've told us today, if I can summarise, about the attack on Mostar, is that you believe that a conflict broke out sometime around the 9th of May. Sometime after that, you saw an order that suggested to you that the ABiH had initiated the attack. That's your testimony, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than that testimony, then, sir, do you have any specific knowledge or information that you can provide the Court, that you can assist the Court with that would conflict with high-level assessments by both the ECMM and UNPROFOR, very clear assessments that the HVO was -- it was the HVO who launched the attack on Mostar in May of 1993, the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I do not have any specific information, especially not that which you are suggesting, and you are saying that the reports of some international organisations were, as you put it, but I really am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't asking you necessarily to agree with me. The Court, the Judges will recall the evidence. I am simply asking you, do you have any information or evidence that you can supply to the Court that will contradict that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: With every ounce of goodwill, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 13 of your statement, can you tell the Court who were these hard line, as you called them, hard-line Muslim fundamentalists that were placed in charge?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Those who, in certain moments towards the end of 1992, tried to replace the persons who were legally elected within the SDA in Konjic, Rama, Mostar and whom we found in different areas when we were there as members of the commission. In their presentations, they simply showed a lack of tolerance. Their rhetoric was very aggressive and they extended messages that are not really fit for this Honorable Court where I am testifying today. It was quite obvious on TV and there are recordings about such areas and their leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the interests of time, I'm only going to ask this to you once. I'd ask you to please answer it directly, and then I will move on in any event. Can you name one of these so-called hard-line Muslim fundamentalists? Just name one for us.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to give you the name but I can give you the surname, his last name is Topcic from Gornji Vakuf. He was present at a meeting of the commission, the joint commission when we had that meeting in Rama.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would consider this man to be a "hard-line Muslim fundamentalist"?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: On the basis of the way he spoke then. On the basis of what he did before and after those events, and equally so because the office of the high representative took away his mandate. Over this past year, he cannot hold any post in the municipal authorities in the Uskoplje and Gornji Vakuf now, and there are probably reasons why they resorted to such a measure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I told you I'd move on, and I will. In paragraph 25, you say there were Muslim commanders in the HVO. Let me ask you again, can you name any of these Muslim commanders who were in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, with pride, my own commander, Jasmin Jaganjac, commander of the municipal staff of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've mentioned him, and wasn't it his view that it was the HVO who had initiated the attack on Gornji Vakuf? Your own superior, the man you just named, it was his view that the HVO initiated the conflict in Gornji Vakuf. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: No, not at all. I doubt this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from any other man, can you name any of the other Muslim commanders in the HVO units?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: High-ranking Colonel Adem, he was from Posavina, lost a son in the BH army attacks on Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was in Posavina?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: He was born in Posavina, but he was in Mostar and later continued as a HVO officer in Posavina. Himzo Azrajic in the Ministry of the Interior units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Mostar or --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: There were a number of captains --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I appreciate you're trying to answer the question I've ask you, but if you would allow me to ask you then, when you name these individuals, what unit -- what particular unit were they in or what area of Bosnia, if you recall? If you can't recall the unit, what area of Bosnia were they assigned to?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Who? The [inaudible] I mentioned, I know them as members of Croat Defence Council units in Mostar. Apart from that, I am sure they have identity cards and documentation, and they can give you the entire structure of the units per area, the -- and chains of command and so forth. I only mentioned a few people with high military ranks, those who are commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these men, were they involved in fighting against the Serbs or were they involved in fighting against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: They did not leave the units of the Croat Defence Council throughout the period, except that Mr. Jasmin Jaganjac, I think on the basis of an agreement between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban, was appointed to the joint command, to its coordinating body, and had its office in Sarajevo. I think that it testifies to his abilities, his moral virtues, and his option for cooperation between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the interests of time, sir, we'll move on. In paragraph 15, you mention something called the MDS. Can you tell the Court, is that the same thing as the Croat-Muslim Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, one in Zagreb -- I think it was up there -- and the other one was founded and functioned under the rules which at that time were provisionally in effect in the area of Herceg-Bosna. They were independent, insofar as the organisation of their statutes are concerned. It was organised and registered in the area of its activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a man associated with that party named Mohamed Zuljic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Could he be from Orasje perhaps?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I can't tell you that right at the moment.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I'd be happy to cooperate. I know a person -- I don't know his name. He came from Posavina, but he was there. He has sort of a dark complexion, but I'm afraid of mixing up and wrongly identifying somebody. But if I may or if you need it, Armin Pohara was another person, Dr. Hamica Alic was another person. There were very many eminent intellectuals who participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You'll have to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me just ask you -- if I can ask that you allow me one more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that party, the Croat-Muslim Democratic Party, ever called simply the Muslim Democratic Party, or wasn't it always the Croat-Muslim Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: One of its names, the one you mention, it was originally which was founded and operated in the Republic of Croatia. Here in the area of Mostar and its broader area, it was the Muslim Democratic Party, the president of which was Dr. Hamica Alic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Court will allow me just to clarify, and it's the last question on the issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't this a group, sir, of in fact Croat people by ethnicity, Croat people who practised the Muslim or Islamic faith?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: One could rightfully say that about those who were in Zagreb. As for those who were active in Mostar and broader areas, one could not say that exactly. They were and are what they say they are and what they were, and I think they are clearly identified by their ethnicity. Contrary to what has just been said, they are not Croats of Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move on, sir. In paragraph 4 of your statement, is it truly your position, sir, that the Bosnian Muslim forces stopped the HVO from relieving Sarajevo, or is that your evidence? Perhaps you didn't say that at all.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're correct, sir. I apologise. In your statement, in paragraph 4 there is the statement, and I'm not quoting it at the moment -- you can certainly have it in front of you -- but it's to the effect that the Bosnian Muslims or the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina stopped or prevented the HVO from relieving Sarajevo. It's at the very end of paragraph 4. Is that your testimony or not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: If I may be allowed, I believe you mention a name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I think you mentioned the name of the commander, Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Be that as it may, sir, my question stands. Is it really your testimony or not, because it's in your statement, sir, but it was not in your testimony this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was in the testimony this morning. The witness expressed that view in terms, and I was going to ask him what his evidence for it was.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Vucina, you would deal with that.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I'm most grateful, Your Honours. According to the direct testimony of the commander who led those units, General Batlak, and now I'm saying a Croat of Muslim faith, he personally told me that from Mr. Sefer Halilovic, he had received not only a message, but according to his testimony, he claims that that message was in writing. According to him, I think that a form of that threat was, "If you pass through here, there will be blood." Your Honours, I also need to mention the following: That person was a general, an honourable man for full cooperation between the Croat and Muslim people, and I believe a year ago he passed away. But I declare under oath before this Honourable Court that I personally heard the statement of such an honourable man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate the Court's correction. We were not clear that it had, in fact, been the testimony. But I certainly accept the Court's view, and that my question, in any event, was the basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only basis for your testimony to that effect, sir, this statement that was apparently made to you by this one individual?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the record is clear, this is reference to an event in June. We all know Sarajevo was under siege for a long time. This particular incident you're telling us about was in June of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Correct. While there was still a chance, had there been any goodwill, a great deal could have been done to de-block Sarajevo, and that is why such an order or such a warning comes as a surprise, that the units led by General Batlak should not advance towards Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more point on that and then we'll move on. Do you know -- be very specific, please, with the Court, if you can, was it the statement that was attributed to Mr. Halilovic that if the HVO forces moved in the direction of Sarajevo, perhaps towards some other objective, perhaps towards some other important Croat position, that they would be stopped? Are you sure that he said, "If you attempt to relieve Sarajevo, you will be stopped"?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Before this Honourable Court, I state that what I heard from the honourable man, General Batlak, was authentically conveyed by me here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You've testified that there were some 14.000 refugees coming from somewhere. In paragraph 14 of your summary, it is said there were 14.000 of them. If you want to look at your statement, that's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, I know, and I said that that figure was even larger. But that was the minimum, that was, which refers to the scope and gravity of these events and happenings, the problems with refugees at the same time 500 metres away, as the crow flies, from the front line. That was a major burden. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was, sir: Where were these refugees from, where were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: From the areas of the municipalities of Gacko, East Herzegovina, occupied and expelled and chased away by the army of JNA, Republika Srpska; area of Bileca; likewise East Herzegovina, expelled by those same units; areas of Nevesinje; likewise --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: -- areas of a part of the municipality of Mostar. Roughly, it's a village on the very front line; likewise to the town itself, and part from southern parts of the municipality of Mostar, south-eastern parts, who were expelled at the very beginning of combat operations towards the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point is, sir, all these refugees came -- were people or citizens, if you will, of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or at least the vast majority of them, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Almost all, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Croats in the area around Mostar and in Central Bosnia, all or most of them were citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both of these groups, at least at that time, both spoke essentially the same language, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: You are very well aware that language is one of the chief features of a people. Yes, we could understand one another, but those are two languages. I cannot deny the right of the Muslim people to have their language, because they want it so and it is their constitutional right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying that we can see, then, that both these groups of people, the refugees and the people in the area in which they were coming, were citizens of the same country, they spoke essentially the same or similar languages? You agree in your statement, in fact, "We agreed to take care of many of them, and that was done." Do you see that in paragraph 14 of your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, I see that with great effort, and I wish to express my great satisfaction that we succeeded in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, in your statement you say: "The ethnic balance was destroyed." My question to you, sir, is: So what? Why was ethnic balance important?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: My answer to that is probably the ensuing events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't my question to you, sir. You said in paragraph 14: "The ethnic balance on the west bank of Mostar was destroyed just as the ethnic balance in Central Bosnia was being destroyed." These were all citizens of the same country, sir. What is the point of saying that? Why have you told this Court that the ethnic balance was destroyed? Why is that even significant?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: They were citizens of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina in those places through which there had been chased away in their places there were the citizens of the municipality of Gacko, citizens of the municipality of Bileca, citizens of the municipality of Trebinje, citizens of the municipality of Nevesinje, and so on and so forth. Why were they expelled? They were the citizens of this state. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in paragraph six that it was clear that the Muslims had made a strategic judgement to commit their many fighting forces to reducing those portions of Central Bosnia that were under Croat control. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you is: Weren't the Croats doing the same thing in many respects, that is to reduce the portions of the country called Bosnia-Herzegovina, reduce the portions of that country that were under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I don't think the interpretation is all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll say it again and perhaps the translation will be -- if you think there is a problem it will come through differently.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't that being done, I think you're right, there may be a portion -- were not the Croats, sir, doing the same thing in seeking to reduce the portion of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Such as, for instance?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's my question. Were not the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Me too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll try one more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I don't think we're going to get much further with this. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it, you say that the Muslims were not satisfied with the land allocated to them under the Vance-Owen Plan. My question to you sir is: Why should they have been satisfied? Do you recall that in fact in many municipalities that were the majority Muslim were being included within the Croat provinces under the plan?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I never claimed that they could be satisfied. I do not deny the right to be dissatisfied. It is an absolute political right and responsibility of their leadership to what they -- to the proposal they made except I think that negotiations had to be conducted and conducted and conducted rather than wage war. And that is what I think generally of the overall internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I do not think that the only responsibility was between these two parties because this deplorable war between victims because both -- both peoples are the victims of a horrible military operation of the Yugoslav People's Army which was not that and, of course, very well equipped army of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying not to interrupt you any more than necessary, but there's --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, that under the Vance-Owen Plan, if you recall, as the number one or Chief of Staff to Mr. Boban, if you know, that under that plan, the Bosnian Croats who were approximately 17 per cent of the population would be given 28 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, but it is also correct that there were 31 Serbs and they were accorded 49 per cent of the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
